1. The gap

0:30

Takeaway

Coordinators are everywhere in fetal cardiology, but nobody has defined which practices matter or how they shape mothers’ experience.

Say out loud

  • CHD is the most common serious birth defect: about 8–9 per 1,000 U.S. live births.
  • Most specialized fetal cardiology programs (79%) already use nurse care coordinators.
  • But there’s no evidence-based framework for which practices they use, how, or what it means for mothers.

2. Study at a glance

0:35

Takeaway

A rigorous qualitative design: mothers’ own accounts, double-coded, then checked with coordinators.

Say out loud

  • Two questions: which coordination practices does a leading prenatal CHD program use, and how do mothers experience them being there or missing?
  • 19 interviews, Oct 2025–Feb 2026, all care in Indiana.
  • Four coders, double-coded to strong agreement. Then we brought the themes back to care coordinators to check them.

To resolve

Kappa: the abstract says coding continued until kappa reached 0.80. The later full-codebook kappa averaged 0.882. Which do we report?

3. Two pathways (core finding)

0:45

Takeaway

At each of six stages, either the care system absorbs the coordination burden or the mother does. The two pathways end in very different places.

Say out loud

  • Walk the spine left to right: diagnosis through birth and beyond, six stages.
  • Top row is when the system carries it. Bottom row is when the mother does.
  • Land on the outcomes: confidence and preparedness vs. chronic stress and exhaustion.
  • The diagnosis is the same in both. What differs is who carries the coordination.

Visual

Paper 1 Figure 2 overview (9/15 draft). Swap in the cleaned-up version.

To resolve

The figure’s stage names differ from the abstract’s practice names (e.g., “Readiness-based information delivery” vs. “Phased post-diagnosis information delivery”). Slides 4–5 use the abstract names. The figure also puts practices 2 and 3 in the opposite order.

1
Proactive coordinator engagement

MOTHER CARRIES ITReferral delayed or fragmented; weeks before specialty contact.
2

SYSTEM CARRIES ITInformation paced to what she is ready to hear.
MOTHER CARRIES ITEverything at once, before she can take it in.

SYSTEM CARRIES ITOne coordinator relays between teams for her.

4. Practices 1–3

0:35

Takeaway

The first three practices cover the weeks right after diagnosis: getting connected fast, not being flooded, and not having to be the messenger.

Say out loud

  • The coordinator reaches out first, before the first clinic visit.
  • Information comes in stages she can absorb, ending in a clear plan.
  • One coordinator is the hub, so she doesn’t relay her own history between teams.

Visual

Cards that zoom in on stages 1–3 of the figure, in the same colors. Other candidate quotes: #34 (“level of coordination with the fetal center group”), #61 (“a huge weight lifted”).

To resolve

Confirm the data supports “24–48 hours” before we present it as a finding.

Then: bring the team together, connect peers, prepare for birth
4
Multidisciplinary team involvement

MOTHER CARRIES ITSeparate visits; she pieces the picture together.
5
Peer support and guided learning
SYSTEM CARRIES ITCurated peer connections and trusted resources.
MOTHER CARRIES ITShe searches alone online, unsure what to trust.
6
Birth preparation

5. Practices 4–6

0:35

Takeaway

The next three practices carry her from understanding the diagnosis to being ready for birth.

Say out loud

  • One day, every specialist at one table, the full picture at once.
  • Connection to families who’ve been there, and to trusted resources.
  • Tours, birth plans, and NICU walkthroughs, so the hospital isn’t a shock.

Visual

Same layout as slide 4. Other candidate quotes: #106 (7 specialists at one table; long, could be trimmed), #57 (support and camaraderie), #29 (learning to advocate).

6. When it was missing

0:30

Takeaway

Coordination gaps weren’t rare edge cases. Mothers described them often, and they cost something.

Say out loud

  • When these practices were missing, mothers described information overload, relaying their own history, and feeling unprepared.
  • Searching alone online came up in 14 of 19 interviews. Information overload came up in 10.

To resolve

The counts come from the draft figure. Re-check them against the final codebook, or keep this slide quote-led with no counts.

Coordination is a teachable model, not luck
“
…after we had gotten the actual CHD diagnosis and had a game plan. I think I could enjoy my pregnancy again.
– Participant #40
Program design
Use the six practices as a blueprint for how fetal cardiac programs run.
Coordinator training
Teach the practices explicitly, so quality doesn’t depend on who you get.
Standard, family-centered support
Make this level of coordination the default for every family.

7. What it means

0:40

Takeaway

These six practices can be taught and standardized. That shapes program design and coordinator training.

Say out loud

  • When the practices were there, mothers could take in information at a manageable pace, trust their care, and draw on their own resilience.
  • That makes this a structured, teachable model that programs can design for and train coordinators in.
  • This is one of the first evidence-based frameworks for prenatal CHD care coordination.

Visual

The title quote on the left. The implication lines are drafted from the abstract’s conclusion; rewrite freely.

Format rules from AHA

  1. PowerPoint or PDF, one approved file. No animations, transitions, hyperlinks, or embedded video/audio.
  2. Audio narration is recorded separately for online viewers. It isn’t used in the live session, so the slides have to stand on their own.
  3. Treat it like a short oral talk. Don’t cut an existing poster into slides.
